extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (researchers, graduate students, and first-time authors) writing or reading mathematical research papers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice on composing, organising, and submitting mathematical research papers, plus complementary guidance on how to read mathematics effectively. Emphasis is on exposition, notation, detail-level, and submission practices for math authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop your own writing style
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone has to develop their own writing style, based on their own strengths and weaknesses, on the subject matter, on the target audience, and sometimes on the target medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is virtually impossible to prescribe rigid rules that encompass all situations and styles; use common sense and tailor style to personal strengths, subject, audience, and medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the introduction to 'sell' the key points
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the introduction to 'sell' the key points of your paper; the results should be described accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction should make the main contributions clear and attractive while remaining accurate about what is proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organise and motivate the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest effort in both organising and motivating the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide structure and motivation so readers understand why results matter and how the paper is arranged; this improves accessibility and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select good notation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose notation that aids clarity and avoids unnecessary cognitive load; good notation helps organisation and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give appropriate amounts of detail
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance between too little detail (leaving gaps) and too much detail (burying main ideas); include enough explanation to be verifiable and comprehensible without overloading the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-optimise the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not over-optimise the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive fine-tuning that consumes disproportionate time for marginal gains in exposition; aim for effective clarity rather than perfection at the cost of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor the paper into smaller pieces (use lemmas)
rubrics_metrics.description: It assists readability if you factor the paper into smaller pieces, for instance by making plenty of lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking arguments into lemmas and modular components helps readers follow complex proofs and locate arguments more easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a rapid prototype first
rubrics_metrics.description: To reduce the time needed to write and organise a paper, write a rapid prototype first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create an initial draft focused on core arguments and results; refine notation, exposition, and structure in subsequent iterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write professionally and in your own voice; target your past self
rubrics_metrics.description: For first time authors especially, it is important to try to write professionally and in one’s own voice; it can also help to make your past self your target audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a professional tone that remains authentic; imagine explaining the paper to your earlier self to ensure clarity and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use natural language, not only symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Take advantage of the English language, and not just rely purely on mathematical symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sentences and exposition to narrate ideas and provide intuition—mathematical symbols alone often fail to communicate structure or motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximise the ratio between results and effort (local maximum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio between results and effort in one’s paper should be at a local maximum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for presentations and selections of results that give readers the most insight for the effort invested; prioritise clarity and impactful results rather than marginal refinements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread and double-check before submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofread and double-check your article before submission; you should be submitting a final draft, not a first draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure correctness, clarity, and polish; fix obvious errors and inconsistencies prior to sending to a journal to respect referees' time and improve acceptance chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit to an appropriate journal
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a venue whose scope and standards match your paper's content and level; targeting the right journal improves the match with referees and readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to resolve 'compilation errors' when reading papers
rubrics_metrics.description: On 'compilation errors' in mathematical reading, and how to resolve them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading, treat formal or typographical inconsistencies as 'compilation errors' to be diagnosed and fixed so the argument compiles logically; see linked commentary for techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use implicit notational conventions as contextual clues when reading
rubrics_metrics.description: On the use of implicit mathematical notational conventions to provide contextual clues when reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and exploit standard but unstated conventions in notation to infer intended meanings and streamline comprehension of arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify 'jumps in difficulty' in arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: On key 'jumps in difficulty' in a mathematical argument, and how finding and understanding them is often key to understanding the argument as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate steps where complexity increases dramatically; focus effort on understanding those hubs of difficulty, as they often control the argument's structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect 'local' and 'global' errors in mathematical papers
rubrics_metrics.description: On 'local' and 'global' errors in mathematical papers, and how to detect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between small (local) mistakes and structural (global) errors; use strategies to spot each and assess their impact on the paper's correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify complicated-looking steps via strategic guesses and temporary notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some general principles (with a worked example) on how to justify a complicated looking step in an argument, for instance by strategically guessing and introducing temporary notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a step seems obscure, try conjecturing intermediate forms or introduce temporary notation to make the logic transparent; this can help both writing and reading complex derivations.
